records.name: Oaxaca
records.current_summary:
In May 2024 the organising brotherhood of a flagship traditional festival in this region circulated a written invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; muxe activists filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body. These festivals are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists - the exclusion is directly visitor-facing.

April 2025 reporting profiles the region as the country's fastest-growing tourist paradise and at the same time its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community: several violent incidents are under investigation with possible municipal-police participation, in municipalities where armed groups operate, and the state's answer has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform. The state human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 discrimination investigations involving LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022, and violence against muxes persists despite the state's international reputation for diversity.

The legal layer points the other way: the state has allowed legal gender recognition since 2019, extended it to age 12 and above by decree in 2021, and a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure. The result is coexistence: a formally protective legal framework alongside customary exclusion enforced at the exact events tourists attend.
records.current_localsOnly: The administrative gender-recognition procedure (12+ since 2021) is a resident route; its openness measures official climate more than it protects a visitor crossing a checkpoint with mismatched documents.

sources.claim: La Tinta Oaxaca (25 May 2024): the organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer Goola 'Lado Sur' festival in Juchitan circulated an invitation stating 'men dressed as women will not be admitted'; muxe activists, incl. defender Felina Santiago (three decades of advocacy), filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body over the transphobic exclusion. Three velas went ahead on 26 May, with muxes affirming they are part of local society and culture.

Trendencias (Apr 2025): profiles Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and simultaneously its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community — violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate; the murdered include muxe Cristian Hernandez Cutino (31) and stylist Zulma Hernandez Mendoza (43). State response has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

El Universal (27 Sep 2026): Oaxaca's human-rights ombudsperson (Defensoria) opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022; violence against muxes persists — e.g. muxe teacher Marimar 'Estrellita' Santiago killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec, Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

HRW 'Gender Recognition in Mexico by State' (11 Mar 2025), Oaxaca row: the 2019 state civil-code reform created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure, extended to age 12+ by decree in 2021, with a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opening the procedure — the documentary layer the summary's 'formally protective framework' claim rests on.

records.name: Puebla
records.current_summary:
Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people; trans women constituted 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year, across at least 17 states reporting victims. Its legal-gender-recognition law (2021) keeps an 18-year minimum-age requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, yet the state congress has still not corrected the text — legislative non-compliance with a final court ruling is itself a hostility signal directly relevant to a visitor whose documents must match presentation. There is no dedicated investigative machinery, no transfeminicide offence, and no state-level enforcement data.

The combination of top-of-table lethality and open defiance of the judiciary distinguishes Puebla from states that simply lack statutes: here a statute exists but the legislature actively refuses to conform it to a binding ruling. Context for comparison: Mexico City, which also had high counts in 2024-25, created a transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocol within months; Estado de México, which likewise defies a Supreme Court ruling on recognition, has at least had a penal-code hate-crime provision covering bias motives since 2021. Puebla has neither the court-compliant text nor any criminal-law protection or enforcement innovation.

sources.claim: Quadratin (16 Jun 2026): of 60 LGBT+ people murdered in Mexico in 2025, 35 were trans women (58.3%), victims across at least 17 states; Puebla recorded the most of any state (7). The piece also notes documented educational and labour inequality against trans women as a standing condition.

HRW 'Gender Recognition in Mexico by State' (11 Mar 2025), Puebla row: the 2021 state congress passed a civil-code reform recognising the right to legal gender recognition and issued a corresponding implementing decree — the recognition regime the summary flags as still carrying the court-voided 18-year minimum.

records.name: Tripura
records.current_summary:
This state shows the country's clearest pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 police reported apprehending 15 Bangladeshi nationals including seven transgender people in separate incidents within 24 hours, one group seized at a highway check post en route to India's financial capital, some described by police as "disguised as third-gender" - the explicit frame that trans presentation is a cover for infiltration. A coordinated November 2024 sweep detained twelve more, including minors and transgender people. The state shares a long, porous international border, which sustains the checkpoint geography. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.

The institutional counterweight is nominal: the state is one of only twelve states/UTs to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but a right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power. On the audited record there is no statute criminalising trans presence here; the documented harm is police practice at the checkpoints.
records.current_localsOnly: Resident-facing: welfare-board machinery and fake-identity-document crackdowns on local residents; the checkpoint sweeps are the visitor-relevant element.
records.current_outOfScope: General border-security enforcement along the Bangladesh frontier (people smuggling, document fraud) affects all travellers and residents of border districts; only the gender-appearance-as-disguise framing is trans-relevant.

sources.claim: Sentinel Assam: Tripura police apprehended 15 Bangladeshi nationals including 7 transgender individuals in separate incidents within 24 hours — bus search at Panisagar checkpoint, North Tripura, on the Assam-Agartala highway; detainees held fake Aadhaar/PAN cards, were en route Mumbai via Guwahati; Tripura shares a 856-km porous border with Bangladesh.

North East Today (2 Aug 2024): at the Panisagar check post, North Tripura district, police detained 7 Bangladeshi nationals — 2 transgender individuals and 5 others described as disguised as third-gender — travelling by bus to Mumbai; case of fraudulent documents and border-crossing routed through the highway checkpoint.

Sentinel Assam (9 Nov 2024): a joint 24-hour operation in Tripura detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals including minors and transgender people — first group of 6 (3 transgender persons) after midnight destined for Mumbai; second group of 6 with 3 children from Khulna at Udaipur Railway Station; local helper Md Hafizur arrested for facilitating movement.

records.name: West Bengal
records.current_summary:
West Bengal replicates the Tripura checkpoint script: South Dinajpur police arrested a Bangladeshi transgender person for allegedly "infiltrating India," treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity; police also detained the e-rickshaw driver who carried her from the border. The state shares a long Bangladesh border and falls within the same policing logic. West Bengal is also one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (3 of 7 nationally), indicating some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime is occurring at a detectable rate.

Against the national 0.43, West Bengal sits −0.09. The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than Tripura's repeated-sweep pattern. Compared to Tripura (0.31), West Bengal's harm is a single documented arrest plus the broader infiltration framing rather than repeated mass operations; compared to Delhi (0.38), which shares the profiling language but also has India's strongest institutional trans presence, West Bengal lacks that offsetting civic infrastructure outside Kolkata.

A welfare board exists (one of 12 states/UTs with a constituted body), but per the RTI investigation it operates without a functioning policy framework. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism documented in Tripura.
records.current_localsOnly: The Transgender Persons Act cases recorded in West Bengal and the state welfare board's nominal operations concern residents' access to protection machinery; the checkpoint arrest pattern is what reaches trans-presenting visitors crossing the land border.
records.current_outOfScope: General cross-border crime and immigration enforcement in the Dinajpur border belt affects all populations; only the trans-appearance-as-infiltration-evidence framing is state-policy relevant to trans travellers.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (access-denied block); the underlying East Bengal report covers South Dinajpur police arresting "Ali Mondal aka Bijli Mondal," a Bangladeshi transgender person from Sirajganj district, for allegedly infiltrating India, along with the e-rickshaw driver who brought her across the border.

Queerbeat crime-data report (30 Jan 2026), West Bengal row: of the 7 Transgender Persons Act cases nationally in 2021, 3 were registered in West Bengal (highest that year alongside Assam/Kerala) — detectable-rate crime plus the report's caveat that national counts are tiny (20 cases 2019-23) from police-registration bias, and 2025 survey prevalence of 27.2% physical / 22.3% sexual violence.

sources.title: The Reality of Transgender Welfare Boards in India: An RTI Investigation
sources.claim: The Quint (5 November 2024) publishes an RTI investigation into transgender welfare boards: West Bengal is one of the 12 states/UTs that notified a board, but the majority of boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since their creation, and the 17 existing boards 'are mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism, or any power', with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people. Supports this record's claim that West Bengal's constituted welfare board operates without a functioning policy framework.

sources.title: Transwoman alleges RPF constable groped her to 'check gender'
sources.claim: Times of India, Kolkata (18 August 2024): a group of trans women heading to RG Kar Medical College filed an FIR alleging an RPF constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them 'to check her gender' and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegations and counter-filed an FIR against the group, while footage showed the trans woman in tears. Documents the state-actor gender-checking conduct this record associates with West Bengal's policing of trans people.

records.name: Punjab
records.current_summary:
In Amritsar — the spiritual centre of the region's dominant faith — Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade at the Rose Garden after "mounting resistance" from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, the faith's highest temporal authority; organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason for cancelling the annual event (Washington Blade, 23 April 2025). No other Punjab-specific law, ordinance or institution affecting trans people appears in the audited sources for this record.

For a trans visitor the documented signal is institutional, not criminal: no statute here targets trans people, but an organised religious authority compelled the cancellation of the region's annual public trans assembly, and the event simply did not happen. Public visibility in Amritsar therefore carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition, and the absence of any recorded state intervention to preserve the event is part of that record.

sources.title: LGBT rights in India - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national-framework page under which a trans visitor in Punjab (India) stands: on September 6, 2018 the Supreme Court's five-judge bench ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts and holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, while preserving the provision for non-consensual acts; in July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omitted Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which the page says bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing. The page carries no Punjab-specific law or institution targeting trans people, consistent with the record's finding that the documented signal in Punjab is institutional rather than criminal.

sources.title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia on India's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab: it was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people, though the page records criticism that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. This protective national framework is the statute a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under and supports the record's statement that no statute in Punjab targets trans people.

records.name: Tamil Nādu
records.current_summary:
Tamil Nadu is India's most protective sub-national regime for trans visitors. It was the first state to introduce a transgender welfare policy (1995), maintains a dedicated Transgender Welfare Board (as the Third Gender Welfare Board since 15 April 2008) within the Social Welfare & Women Empowerment Department, and adopted a comprehensive State Policy for Transgender Persons in 2025. On 4 August 2025, the Madras High Court (WP 7284 of 2021) expressly commended the policy as "a victory for transgender and intersex persons after their long struggle" — active judicial confirmation of executive protection is rare and meaningful for a visitor's institutional recourse. Tamil Nadu was the only state recording a Transgender Persons Act case in 2020 (1 of 1 nationally) and logged 7 of the 11 national cases in 2023 — its courts are demonstrably being used.

Against the national 0.43, Tamil Nadu sits +0.10. The state has a functioning (by comparison) policy apparatus, court validation, and the Thirunangai/Thirunambi administrative categories embedded in governance. Compared to Kerala (0.50), Tamil Nadu adds the explicit court commendation and longer institutional history; compared to Punjab (0.35), which saw a religious authority veto trans public assembly, Tamil Nadu's state machinery actively protects it. A complicating signal exists — Hindu transgender devotees in Madurai announced a fast in December 2025 over temple lamp-lighting decisions — but this reflects trans people as political actors in state governance, not state suppression of them.
records.current_localsOnly: The board's resident-facing machinery — membership ID cards, free surgery, housing, scholarships, state employment quotas — benefits trans residents of Tamil Nadu; what a visitor encounters is the institutional climate these signal.

sources.claim: Official Tamil Nadu transgender-welfare portal: publishes the gender-change application kit (affidavit form, certificate of identity for change of gender, membership ID relaxation, user manuals) and documents the state regime — first Indian state with a transgender welfare policy, free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, housing and citizenship-scheme access, and the thirunangai/thirunambi administrative categories embedded in governance.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (never cached); the underlying document is the Madras High Court order of 4 August 2025 (WP 7284 of 2021) noting with approval that the state brought into effect the Tamil Nadu State Policy for Transgender Persons 2025, calling it "a victory for transgender and intersex persons after their long struggle" and expressly commending the government.

Queerbeat crime-data report (30 Jan 2026), Tamil Nadu rows: the only state with a Transgender Persons Act case in 2020 (1 of 1 nationally) and in 2022 (1), and 7 of the 11 national cases in 2023 — courts demonstrably reachable in this state, against the report's registration-bias caveat.

records.name: Kerala
records.current_summary:
Kerala holds a constituted Transgender Welfare Board — one of the 12 states/UTs reported to the federal parliament in December 2021 as having set one up under the national trans-protection rules (PIB) — and its law-enforcement machinery is measurably engaged: the state registered 2 of the 7 national cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 and 4 of the 11 recorded in 2023, among the highest sub-national totals in those years (queerbeat data report, 30 January 2026).

That activity should be read with the source's own caveat: national recording is sparse (20 cases across 2019–23) because of police registration bias, against survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence (2025 Transgender Health study, n=4,964). Registered cases therefore evidence a system that at least accepts complaints, not rarity of violence. No Kerala-specific restriction is documented; for a visitor the picture is one of institutional recognition machinery in a state where such machinery exists and is used.
records.current_localsOnly: The overseas scholarship scheme and board benefit measures are resident-facing programmes; their visitor-facing content is the signal of state commitment.

sources.claim: Queerbeat crime-data report (30 Jan 2026), Kerala rows: 2 of the 7 national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023 (joint-highest with Tamil Nadu) — among the highest sub-national totals, with the report's caveat that national counts are tiny from police-registration bias.

PIB federal reply (Dec 2021): Kerala is among the 12 states/UTs reported to parliament as having constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules — the named-board claim the record summary rests on.

records.name: Assam
records.current_summary:
Assam appears in national crime records with 2 of the 7 cases registered under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021, and none in the 2023 tally (queerbeat data report, 30 January 2026) — which itself cautions that national counts are tiny (20 cases 2019–23) because of police registration bias, with 2025 survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence. Recorded cases prove the complaint system is reachable, not that violence is uncommon.

In the December 2021 federal reply listing the 12 states/UTs that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards (PIB), Assam is not among them — i.e., no state welfare machinery stood in place as of that date. No Assam-specific protective or restrictive statute, ordinance or checkpoint operation is documented in the audited sources; the record supports a thin official-visibility finding balanced against the region-wide caveats, nothing more.

sources.claim: Queerbeat crime-data report (30 Jan 2026), Assam rows: 2 of the 7 Transgender Persons Act cases registered nationally in 2021 fell in Assam, none in the 2023 tally — complaint system reachable; report cautions national counts are tiny (20 cases 2019-23) due to police-registration bias, with 2025 survey prevalence at 27.2% physical / 22.3% sexual violence.

PIB federal reply (Dec 2021): the reply to parliament names the 12 states/UTs that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under the 2019 Rules — Assam is absent from that list, evidencing the record's 'no state welfare machinery as of Dec 2021' claim.
